meta.description: Harry S. Truman, off the cuff, in Washington on 11 April 1958 — with a newspaper report the next morning and a Library of Congress citation to match.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A politician is a man who understands government, and it takes a politician to run a government. A statesman is a politician who's been dead 10 or 15 years'?
meta.ogDescription: Truman said it before the Reciprocity Club on 11 April 1958, reported by the New York World-Telegram and Sun the following day.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Truman said this in impromptu remarks before the Reciprocity Club in Washington, D.C. on 11 April 1958, five years out of office, and the New York World-Telegram and Sun carried it the next morning. The citation is set out in the Library of Congress’s own reference work Respectfully Quoted ↗, which records the venue, the date and that newspaper report of 12 April 1958. The full remark begins with a line usually dropped in circulation: “I’m proud that I’m a politician.”

source.excerpt: “I’m proud that I’m a politician. A politician is a man who understands government, and it takes a politician to run a government. A statesman is a politician who’s been dead 10 or 15 years.”
trail: Truman’s English Wikiquote page ↗ carries the sentence in its sourced Quotes section — not among the attributed, disputed or misattributed entries — and cites impromptu remarks before the Reciprocity Club, Washington, D.C., 11 April 1958.

We checked that citation against the source it rests on rather than taking it on trust. Respectfully Quoted: A Dictionary of Quotations Requested from the Congressional Research Service ↗, edited by Suzy Platt and published by the Library of Congress in 1989, carries the quotation at entry 1405, and its full text ↗ gives the citation in full: “harry s. truman, impromptu remarks before the Reciprocity Club, Washington, D.C., April 11, 1958, as reported by the New York World-Telegram and Sun, April 12, 1958, p. 4.”

The wording in that entry matches the line as it circulates today, word for word, including the contraction in “who’s been dead 10 or 15 years” — so this is one of the rare famous one-liners that has not drifted. Truman’s biography ↗ places him in exactly the position the joke implies in 1958: a former president, five years out of office, still very much alive.
source.excerptNote: The opening sentence is the one that gets cut, and it changes the joke: Truman is not sneering at politicians, he is defending them, and the crack about statesmen is the defence.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.heading: About Harry S. Truman
author.bio: Harry S. Truman was a Missouri farmer, a failed haberdasher and a machine-politics county judge before the Senate, the vice-presidency, and then the presidency on Franklin Roosevelt’s death in 1945. He never lost the habit of speaking like someone who had run for county office, which is why so many of his lines survive: he talked in finished sentences that happened to be funny. This one he delivered in 1958, out of office and unbothered.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody else gets credited with this one, but it is routinely quoted in a shape that inverts its meaning.

items.why: Dropping “I’m proud that I’m a politician” turns a defence of politicians into a sneer at them. Truman was doing the opposite.
He said it in April 1958, five years after leaving the White House — the citation is explicit ↗ about the date.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution itself is sound: the Library of Congress reference ↗ names the occasion, the date and the newspaper that reported it the following morning.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Truman spent his career being told he was a politician rather than a statesman, usually by people who meant it as an insult, and this is his answer to all of them at once. The definition he gives of a politician is flatly complimentary — a man who understands government — and the punchline does the demolition: a statesman is just a politician who has been safely dead long enough to be admired.

He was well placed to make the joke in 1958. He had been out of office for five years and was, by the terms of his own definition, still disqualified from statesmanship on the only ground that counts — he was alive.
context.pull: A statesman is a politician who has been safely dead long enough to be admired.
